PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 49 — Lesson 73: Men’s Health Assessment

FNP-level goal: Evaluate lower urinary tract symptoms, hematuria, scrotal/testicular symptoms, sexual concerns, and prostate-related presentations using stability, an inclusive history, focused examination, targeted diagnostics, appropriate referral, and a safety-first disposition. Recognize time-sensitive acute scrotum, urinary retention, severe infection, significant bleeding, concerning mass, and cardiometabolic risk patterns that cannot safely wait for routine follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate storage, voiding, and post-void lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) without assuming every symptom is benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
  • Construct a safety-focused differential for hematuria, acute urinary retention, scrotal pain, testicular mass, erectile dysfunction (ED), and sexual symptoms.
  • Perform a consent-based, trauma-informed, clinically purposeful male genitourinary examination and document limitations.
  • Select testing to answer a defined question: urinalysis, culture, post-void residual, STI testing, renal studies, imaging, scrotal ultrasound, and specialty referral.
  • Recognize emergency and expedited-urology patterns, including possible torsion, sepsis/obstruction, acute retention, gross hematuria with instability, and a new testicular mass.
  • Connect sexual and urinary symptoms to diabetes, vascular disease, medication effects, neurologic disease, mood, relationship context, and preventive care.

Part 1 — Begin With Stability and the Time-Critical Differential

Men’s-health symptoms range from common chronic bothersome conditions to organ-threatening or life-threatening emergencies. First assess vital signs, pain severity and trajectory, ability to void, mental status, hydration, fever/systemic illness, bleeding severity, vomiting, and the patient’s ability to obtain prompt follow-up. A focused symptom label such as “BPH,” “UTI,” or “epididymitis” must never replace this first safety assessment.

Emergency patterns include sudden severe unilateral scrotal/testicular pain, especially with nausea/vomiting; acute inability to void with painful distention or systemic illness; fever/rigors with obstruction or flank pain; hypotension, syncope, or significant active bleeding; severe genital/perineal pain with toxic appearance; and chest symptoms or unstable physiology accompanying sexual-health concerns. Stabilization and emergency transfer take priority over completing a detailed office examination or waiting for routine outpatient imaging.

Part 2 — Build an Inclusive, Confidential History

Ask permission before discussing urinary, genital, reproductive, and sexual concerns. Explain why the questions matter and use the patient’s words for body parts, gender, partners, and sexual practices. Offer privacy and confidentiality within applicable law. A complete history includes onset, duration, progression, pain quality/location/radiation, fever, trauma, urinary pattern, gross versus microscopic blood, discharge/lesions, STI exposure/testing, fertility goals, medication/substance use, prior surgery/instrumentation, neurologic disease, diabetes, kidney disease, anticoagulants, cancer history, and family history.

For sexual symptoms, ask about desire, erection quality, ejaculation, orgasm, pain, curvature, morning/nocturnal erections when relevant, partner/relationship context, anxiety/depression, sleep, alcohol/recreational substances, and safety. Sexual history is clinical data, not a moral test. Do not assume risk or anatomy from age, identity, relationship status, or appearance.

Part 3 — LUTS: Describe the Pattern Before Naming the Cause

Lower urinary tract symptoms describe a symptom complex, not one diagnosis. Storage symptoms include urgency, frequency, nocturia, and urge incontinence. Voiding symptoms include weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, straining, and a sense of incomplete emptying. Post-micturition symptoms include dribbling or a persistent incomplete-emptying sensation. Clarify baseline function, fluid/caffeine/alcohol use, nocturnal urine production, constipation, sleep apnea symptoms, diuretics and timing, and impact on sleep, work, driving, and quality of life.

BPH is common, but LUTS may also arise from urinary infection, prostatitis, urethral stricture, bladder dysfunction/overactivity, neurogenic bladder, medication effects, diabetes, heart failure/nocturnal fluid redistribution, stones, malignancy, or another process. The FNP task is to identify the symptom pattern, likely mechanism, red flags, and next diagnostic question rather than reflexively labeling every older patient’s symptoms as prostate enlargement.

Part 4 — Acute Retention and Obstruction: Do Not Miss the Consequences

Acute urinary retention may present with inability to void, painful suprapubic fullness, restlessness, overflow leakage, lower-abdominal pain, or an atypical presentation in older adults. Consider obstruction, medication effects, constipation, infection/inflammation, neurologic disease, recent surgery/anesthesia, and impaired detrusor function. Fever, flank pain, vomiting, kidney injury concern, severe pain, altered mental status, or sepsis physiology increases urgency.

Objective assessment may include a bladder scan or post-void residual (PVR) when available and clinically appropriate. A PVR helps answer whether incomplete emptying or retention is present; it does not independently establish the cause. A patient who cannot void, is in severe pain, appears systemically ill, or may have obstructed infection needs urgent/emergency evaluation rather than a delayed outpatient trial-and-error plan.

Part 5 — BPH and Prostate Assessment: Be Specific and Patient-Centered

BPH refers to benign enlargement of prostatic tissue, while LUTS can be related to the bladder, prostate, urethra, or other conditions. For bothersome LUTS possibly attributed to BPH, a focused history, physical examination, symptom assessment such as IPSS, and urinalysis help establish a baseline and identify alternate explanations. PVR and uroflowmetry may be helpful in selected patients, especially when retention or poor emptying is a concern.

Discuss examination choices and obtain consent before a digital rectal examination (DRE). A DRE can add selected information but is not a stand-alone cancer test and should not be forced or used without explaining the purpose. Screening and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) decisions require current guideline-informed shared decision-making that considers age, life expectancy, risk, prior results, symptoms, and the patient’s values. A current symptom still requires diagnostic evaluation even if prior screening was normal.

Part 6 — Hematuria: Localize, Risk-Stratify, and Close the Loop

First confirm what the patient is seeing: red/pink/brown urine, clots, bleeding from the urethra, rectal bleeding, or another source. Ask about dysuria, urgency, flank pain, colic, fever, trauma, recent exercise, anticoagulants, smoking exposure, occupational risks, stones, infection, renal disease, pelvic radiation, prior instrumentation, and unexplained weight loss. Urinalysis with microscopy can help distinguish red cells from pigment and identify infection/protein/glucose clues, but a single reassuring result does not replace follow-up when the history is concerning.

Hematuria may reflect infection, stone disease, glomerular disease, trauma, medication-associated bleeding, or urinary-tract malignancy. Anticoagulant use may increase visible bleeding but must not be used to dismiss a potentially important underlying lesion. Gross hematuria with clots, inability to void, significant anemia symptoms, unstable vital signs, severe pain, fever/obstruction, or ongoing heavy bleeding requires urgent assessment. Document result ownership, the next test/referral, and exact return precautions.

Part 7 — Acute Scrotum: Torsion Is a Diagnostic-Safety Emergency

Sudden unilateral scrotal or testicular pain is an acute-scrotum presentation until a clinician has safely evaluated time-sensitive causes. Testicular torsion threatens blood supply to the testis and can present with abrupt severe pain, nausea/vomiting, swelling, or an abnormal testicular position. Epididymitis, incarcerated hernia, trauma, torsion of an appendage, stone-related referred pain, tumor, and other disorders can mimic each other. A history or physical finding alone cannot safely rule out torsion when the presentation is concerning.

Do not delay emergency disposition to obtain a routine office test. In an equivocal but stable setting, urgent Doppler scrotal ultrasound and urologic/emergency evaluation may be part of the pathway; the exact route depends on local resources and clinical concern. The safety principle is simple: suspected torsion needs immediate emergency evaluation because a delay can result in loss of organ function.

Part 8 — Testicular Mass, Swelling, and Chronic Scrotal Symptoms

A painless testicular lump, persistent enlargement, change in consistency, unexplained heaviness, or new scrotal fluid deserves timely clinical evaluation. Benign conditions can cause similar symptoms, but malignancy cannot be excluded by reassurance, age alone, or a brief external inspection. Examine only with consent and privacy; compare sides, assess tenderness, skin change, inguinal findings when appropriate, and whether the finding seems intratesticular versus extratesticular. Avoid declaring a mass benign without appropriate imaging and specialty follow-up.

Scrotal ultrasound is commonly used to characterize a suspected testicular/scrotal mass. A symptom that persists, changes, or is accompanied by systemic symptoms needs a closed-loop plan. Communicate clearly: “The test is to define the structure; a normal feeling examination does not replace the recommended diagnostic pathway.”

Part 9 — Erectile Dysfunction Is a Whole-Patient Clinical Signal

ED is difficulty getting or keeping an erection adequate for sexual activity. It is not an inevitable or trivial consequence of aging. Vascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, sleep disorders, neurologic disease, hormonal disorders, pelvic surgery, medication effects, tobacco/alcohol/substance exposure, depression/anxiety, and relationship factors can contribute. Often more than one mechanism is present.

Evaluate ED with a medical, sexual, mental-health, and medication history plus targeted examination and testing based on the patient’s context. It can be an opportunity to review blood pressure, glycemic status, cardiovascular symptoms/exercise tolerance, lipids, sleep, depression, substance use, and medication adverse effects. Do not promise that a single medication is appropriate before assessing contraindications, drug interactions, cardiovascular stability, and the patient’s goals. Follow current guidelines, scope, and collaborating/specialty pathways for treatment decisions.

Part 10 — Focused Examination: Consent, Purpose, and Limits

Explain what you plan to examine, why, who will be present, and how the patient can pause or stop. Offer a chaperone according to policy and patient preference, protect draping/privacy, and document consent, relevant declined components, and limitations. A focused examination may include general appearance, vital signs, abdomen/suprapubic area, costovertebral angle, external genital skin/penis/scrotum/testes, inguinal region, focused neurologic/vascular findings, and DRE when clinically indicated and consented.

Do not let a declined or incomplete examination produce false reassurance. If a patient is unstable, in severe pain, at risk of torsion/obstruction/sepsis, or needs imaging beyond clinic capability, the correct action is a higher-level diagnostic pathway—not pressure to complete every maneuver.

Part 11 — Testing Should Answer a Clinical Question

Choose tests based on the presentation. Urinalysis and culture can address infection/hematuria questions; STI testing can be site- and exposure-specific; PVR can assess emptying; renal function/electrolytes may matter with suspected obstruction or systemic disease; and targeted glucose/endocrine/cardiovascular evaluation may support an ED assessment. Scrotal ultrasound helps characterize a mass or acute-scrotum concern when it will not delay required emergency care. Imaging, PSA, and referral are not “routine boxes”; each should answer a specific question and have an owner for reviewing results.

Before ending the visit, identify what result would change disposition, what still has not been excluded, when/how the patient receives results, and what symptoms require immediate care. This closed-loop approach prevents a negative partial test from becoming an accidental end point.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Sudden Scrotal Pain

A 17-year-old develops abrupt severe unilateral testicular pain with nausea during class. He appears distressed and cannot tolerate a detailed examination.

FNP reasoning: this is an acute-scrotum/torsion pattern. Arrange immediate emergency evaluation. Do not delay for routine outpatient ultrasound, STI testing, or a complete clinic examination.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: LUTS, Retention, and Fever

A 69-year-old has worsening weak stream and incomplete emptying, then develops inability to void, painful suprapubic distention, fever, and malaise.

FNP reasoning: the presentation is no longer routine chronic LUTS. Consider retention with infection/obstruction and possible systemic illness. Assess stability and arrange urgent/emergency evaluation; do not simply start a chronic-LUTS plan and wait weeks.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Hematuria Does Not Explain Itself

A 58-year-old who smokes reports visible blood in urine without dysuria. They take an anticoagulant and have unintentionally lost weight.

FNP reasoning: medication use can contribute to bleeding but does not establish the cause. Confirm and localize the bleeding, assess stability, obtain appropriate initial studies, and ensure a timely risk-based urologic/diagnostic pathway with documented follow-up.

Part 15 — Clinical Case: ED and Cardiometabolic Risk

A 54-year-old reports gradually worsening erections. They also have untreated hypertension, diabetes, exertional chest pressure, and use several medications.

FNP reasoning: ED may have vascular, metabolic, medication, and psychosocial contributors. The exertional chest symptom is a separate potential safety issue. Assess cardiovascular stability and medication interactions before considering symptom-directed therapy, and address risk factors through an appropriate current-guideline pathway.

FNP Men’s-Health Assessment Framework

  1. Start with stability: vital signs, severe pain, fever/toxicity, ability to void, bleeding, vomiting, and hemodynamics.
  2. Describe—not label—the symptom pattern: storage/voiding/post-void symptoms, hematuria features, scrotal timing, sexual function, and trajectory.
  3. Build a broad differential: bladder/prostate/urethra, kidney, infection, stones, neurologic, vascular/endocrine, medication, STI, trauma, malignancy, and emergency causes.
  4. Use consent-based examination: privacy, explanation, chaperone option, patient control, documented findings and limitations.
  5. Test with a question: UA/culture, PVR, renal studies, STI testing, ultrasound, cardiovascular/endocrine evaluation, or specialty assessment as indicated.
  6. Escalate red flags: suspected torsion, acute retention, obstructed infection/sepsis, unstable/gross hematuria, concerning mass, severe genital/perineal infection, or cardiopulmonary instability.
  7. Close the loop: result owner, referral access, return precautions, and patient understanding.

High-Yield Summary

LUTS: classify storage, voiding, and post-void symptoms; BPH is common but not the only cause.
Retention: inability to void, painful distention, infection/systemic symptoms, or kidney-risk context needs urgent assessment.
Hematuria: confirm/localize it and evaluate risk; anticoagulation does not explain away a concerning cause.
Acute scrotum: sudden unilateral severe pain, especially with nausea/vomiting, is torsion until safely evaluated—do not delay emergency care.
Testicular mass: a painless lump or persistent change requires timely diagnostic imaging/specialty pathway.
ED: assess vascular, metabolic, neurologic, hormonal, medication, mental-health, and relationship contributors; it can reveal broader health risk.
FNP standard: combine patient-centered consent, physiology, diagnostic humility, targeted testing, disposition, and closed-loop follow-up.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Assessment, imaging, laboratory testing, PSA decisions, medication choices, referral, emergency disposition, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
